So, the fly is not a trivial thing as you suppose. Rather, even smaller than it are the mosquito and the microbe, and others that are not seen with the naked eye, all creatures of Allah, containing secrets that point to His power, may He be exalted.

As He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example — that of a mosquito or what is above it.﴾ (2:26), meaning, what is above it in smallness. You may reflect on the mosquito, which is smaller in size than the fly, and how it has a fine proboscis that penetrates the skin and sucks the blood, which you cannot extract except with difficulty; and the microbe, which you cannot see with your naked eye, yet it creeps into the body, makes it ill, undermines its structure, and may end in death.

So, in these creatures that seem contemptible to you there are lessons and signs, but none understands them except those who have knowledge. Most of these signs and secrets were discovered by people who were not believers in Allah. Some of them understood them and believed, while others did not understand them and remained in their disbelief, even though they were the most worthy of people to believe in Allah, because they possess the knowledge by which they discover the secrets of the Creator in creation. Therefore, it has come in a report: "The true scholar is the one who knows what He created, and why He created it."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

{Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.}

The Truth, glorified is He, wished to demonstrate to us the absoluteness of His power, exalted is He, so He said: ﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth...﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:44]. Creation (khalq) is the bringing into existence of that which did not exist, but for a specific purpose and for a task it performs. If you were to make something merely as it happens, without any aim behind it, it would not be called creation.

This matter of creation is the only one that the disbelievers acknowledged for Allah, exalted is He. When He asked them: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah..."﴾ [Luqman 31:25]. Why did they acknowledge this one in particular? And why did it silence them?

This is not strange from them, because we observe that everyone who brings something new into the universe is eager to attribute it to himself, and to show people his efforts and expertise, and that he invented such-and-such or discovered such-and-such, like the one who discovered electricity or invented the telephone or the television.

We still remember until now the law of buoyancy of Archimedes and the law of gravitation of Newton, and people now register patents so that no one steals another's efforts, and so that the fruit of the genius of those of intellectual superiority and brilliance is preserved for them.

Likewise, the Arabs of old used to mention the merit of the one who deserved merit, so much so that they would say: So-and-so was the first to say, for example, "amma ba'd" (1). And so-and-so was the first to do such-and-such.

Thus, we know the first ones in every field, and we attribute every craft, every invention and discovery to its owner, and indeed we immortalize his memory and erect a statue for him, etc.

So then: what about the Greatest Creator, glorified is He, who created the heavens and the earth and what is in them and who is in them? Is it not His right that He announce Himself? Is it not His right over His servants that they acknowledge Him as the Creator? Especially since the creation of the heavens and the earth was not claimed by anyone for himself, and no contender disputed the Truth in it. Then a messenger from Allah, exalted is He, came to us informing us of this reality, and no one opposed it. The claim is established for its owner until someone opposes it.

We have illustrated this matter, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness, with a group who sat in a gathering. When their assembly dispersed, the owner of the house found a wallet belonging to one of them. He asked them: "Whose wallet is this?" They all said: "It is not mine." Then one of them said: "It is mine." Would the owner of the house doubt that it belongs to the one who claimed it?

And you may ask: since the Truth asked them ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth?...﴾ [Luqman 31:25] and they said "Allah," why does Allah mention this matter? They said: The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, does not intend by this verse to inform us that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth; rather He intends to inform us that the creation of the heavens and the earth is with truth. And truth (al-haqq) is that which is firm and does not change, in accordance with the wisdom attached to everything in existence. So when we look at the creation of the heavens and the earth, we find it firm, nothing in it having changed.

Therefore He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind...﴾ [Ghafir 40:57].

The heavens and the earth are a tremendous, mighty creation, such that if you compared it with the creation of man, the creation of man would be easier. Consider, for example, the lifespan of the heavens and the earth and the lifespan of man: the longest lifespans of humans known to us until now is the lifespan of Noah, peace be upon him, and after this lifespan, which we see as long, he ended in death. The lifespan of man is known to be one year, or a thousand years, but he must die.

As for the heavens and the earth and what is in them of creatures, they were created to serve man. The servant lives longer than the one served. The sun, for example, Allah created it millions of years ago, and it remains as it is, unchanged, and has not deviated from its task. Likewise the moon: ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by precise reckoning﴾ [al-Rahman 55:5].

That is, by precise calculation. Therefore they say: an eclipse of the sun or of the moon will occur on such a day at such an hour, and at the same time an eclipse of the sun or the moon actually occurs, which indicates that they were created with a wondrous, precise reckoning. It is enough that we set our clocks by the sun, for example. And despite what is known of the great size of the sun and the moon, they travel in orbits and spheres without collision, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Each in an orbit they swim﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:33].

All of this is part of the meaning of "created the heavens and the earth with truth": that is, with a firm, precise, regulated order that does not change or differ in any of its manifestations. As for you, O human, you can change, because Allah has given you choice, so you may obey or disobey, believe or, Allah forbid, disbelieve. But the creation of the heavens and the earth came in the form of compulsion and subjection, although they are chosen by the general law and the first choice, where He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:72].

So then: they were given the choice, and they chose not to choose, and they departed from their own desire to the desire of their Lord.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:44]. Why did He say "for the believers," although it is a sign for all people? And Allah had earlier addressed the disbelievers: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth?...﴾ (Luqman). Why does He specify the believers here and not the disbelievers?

They said: There is a difference between the creation of the heavens and the earth, and their being created with truth. Everyone believes that they are created, but only the believers are those who know that they are created with truth.

(1) On the authority of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "The first to say 'amma ba'd' was Dawud the Prophet, peace be upon him." He said: and it is "Fasl al-Khitab." Recorded by Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Awa'il (hadith 191) and al-Tabarani in al-Awa'il (40). al-Suyuti ascribed it in al-Wasa'il (117) to Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami, from Abu Musa.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 29, verse 45:

The Truthful and Glorified One says:

{Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book,
and establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer forbids
immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of God
is greater. And God knows what you do.} (45)

After God, exalted is He, mentioned some of the processions of the messengers: Abraham, Moses, Noah, Salih, Hud, Lot, and Shu'ayb, then He spoke of those who denied these messengers, ﴿So each We seized for his sin...﴾ (40) [al-'Ankabut]. He, glorified is He, wished to console His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, so that he would not be disturbed, nor exhausted, nor wear himself out over the stance of the disbelievers who deny Him, who turn people away from the way of God, and who stand against the call with hostility.

So He said to him, consoling him: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut]. That is: do not grieve, O Muhammad, for you have with you all the intimacy, the intimacy that never ends, and it is the Book of God and His miracle which He sent down to you. So occupy yourself with it, for with every recitation of it you will find tranquility with your Lord.

And if those who lived alongside you did not believe in it, and did not turn to the aspects of its inimitability, then persist in its recitation, perhaps God will bring from these people a progeny whose hearts are purified to receive the transmission from heaven, so they will believe in what these people denied. The command to recite is for the preservation of the miracle.

﴿Recite...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut]: read and do not weaken, and do not despair, for the Qur'an is a solace for yourself. Because whoever sends a messenger from among mankind with something, or regarding some matter, and then he is denied, returns to the one who sent him. So since your people have denied you, return to Me by listening to My Book, which I have sent down as a miracle for you, supporting you, so that they will believe in it.

There is a difference between the agent and the recipient, and the Qur'an clarifies this matter. Among people, when they hear the Qur'an, their hearts humble before it and their skins shiver; and among them are those who, when they hear it, say in mockery ﴿What did he just say?﴾ (16) [Muhammad], belittling the status of the Qur'an and the status of the Messenger of God.

Then the Qur'an establishes this reality: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing; and as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness¹ and it is for them blindness...﴾ (44) [Fussilat].

So: the Qur'an is one, but the reception of the Qur'an differs. The determining factor is the clarity of reception, since the transmission is one. Would you accuse the broadcasting station if the radio you have is broken and does not receive its transmission?

Likewise, whoever wishes to receive the transmission of heaven must prepare an attentive ear and a pure heart, unclouded by what contradicts the transmission of heaven. You must first expel from yourself whatever opposes the Qur'an, then receive the word of God and be affected by it.

We have previously given an example of the difference in the affected thing acted upon: one who blows on his hands in cold weather for the purpose of warming them, and one who blows on tea, for example, to cool it. This is for heat, and that is for cold; the action is one, but the affected thing differs.

So the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut]: this is the distinguishing feature of your miracle, O Muhammad, that you can repeat it at any time, recite it as you wish, and that whoever hears it after you can recite it as well, and it will continue to be recited until the Day of Resurrection.

As for the miracles of the earlier messengers, they were specific to those who witnessed the miracle; if one who witnessed it died, no one would know of it after them, even one who was contemporary with it but did not see it. Those who lived at the time, for example, of the transformation of Moses' staff into a serpent, but did not witness that event, what do they have of this miracle? Nothing, except that we believe in it and accept it, because the Qur'an has informed us of it.

So: the miracles of the earlier peoples come like a single snapshot, much like a match that lights once: whoever saw it saw it, and the matter ends. But the Qur'an has told us of all the miracles of the earlier messengers. So consider what good has reached all the messengers from our master, the Messenger of God, and how the Qur'an has immortalized their remembrance, and how their miracles have extended through the extension of his miracle.

Thus it is as if the Qur'an has conferred a favour upon all the messengers and upon all the miracles. Therefore the Exalted said of the Qur'an: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian over it...﴾ (48) [al-Ma'idah].

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And establish the prayer...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut]. It is known that "recite" (ittlu): recitation is a statement of the tongue's action, and ﴿establish...﴾ (45) is an action of the limbs. Man has many limbs, of which five are well known: the eye for sight, the ear for hearing, the nose for smell, the tongue for taste, and the fingertips for touch.

They said, as a precaution, that the five apparent limbs are these; and indeed it has become evident, with the advance of the sciences, that they have discovered in man other senses and means of perception not known before, such as the muscular sense by which you gauge the weight of things. Otherwise, by which of your five senses would you know weight before lifting the object from the ground?

And like the sense of "thickness" (al-bayn), by which you can distinguish the thickness of things between your fingers. For example, when you go to a cloth merchant, you take the cloth between your fingers and rub it gently, and you can tell that this one is thicker than that.

And among the remarkable matters concerning the limbs is that the tongue takes half of all the limbs. The action of the five senses is called "work" (amal), and work is divided into either speech (qawl) or deed (fi'l). Every movement of a limb to perform a task is called work, but the work of the tongue is called speech, while that of the other limbs is called deed.

The tongue has taken this status because through it comes warning from the Truth, through it comes good tidings, and through it comes the delivery from the Messenger. Therefore the Truthful and Glorified One says: ﴿O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ (2) [al-Saff].

He did not say "what you do not work," because speech is paired with deed, and both are work, and work is by the intention of the heart.

But why did He choose prayer from among the actions of the limbs? They said: because it is the peak of action, as the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, named it: "Prayer is the pillar of the religion,"² and through it we distinguish the believer from the disbeliever. The question remains: why did prayer take this status among the pillars of Islam?

We wish to point out here that the adversaries of Islam, and some of its own people who fear its revival lest it bring an end to their authority, tyranny, and oppression, want to confine Islam to its five pillars. If you affirm this statement, they will not confront you, and you are free within the framework of these pillars of Islam. But beware of saying that Islam came to organize the movement of life, for their interest lies in confining Islam to its pillars alone.

These people did not understand that the pillars are not the whole of Islam; rather they are its foundations and principles upon which its structure stands. But they want to isolate Islam from the movement of life. So we say to them: yes, these are the pillars of Islam, but Islam encompasses everything in our lives, from the summit of belief in our saying "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God," to removing harm from the road; for Islam is a religion that embraces all the affairs of life, and how could it not, when it teaches us the simplest things in our lives?

Do you not see how it concerns itself with the rulings on relieving oneself and entering the lavatory, and what relates to them of etiquette and rulings? Do you not see that the muhtasib³ charged with overseeing the markets and implementing the rulings of God's method on earth, if he sees a butcher blowing into his slaughtered animal with his mouth, executes this animal, because the air used to blow it is unhealthy air: it is exhaled breath laden with carbon dioxide, and may carry other harmful gases that will inevitably pass into the meat of the animal?

Likewise, it is among his duties to pass by the barbers, inspecting their cleanliness and freedom from disease; and if he smells garlic or onion on one of them, for example, he orders the closing of his shop and that he not work that day, so that people are not harmed by his smell.

So what law is this that safeguards people's well-being and feelings to this extent? It is the religion of God and His method, which leaves neither small nor great in the movement of life without establishing for it rulings and etiquette. Is such a law to be cut off from the movement of life and restricted to matters of worship alone?

When you look at the troubles of the world today, leaving aside the developed world, you will find that its troubles are economic; and if you traced the causes, you would find them traceable to abandoning God's method and suspending His rulings. By God, if they had taken in their economic crisis the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "We are a people who do not eat until we are hungry, and when we eat, we do not eat until we are full,"⁴

if they had acted upon this and taken their Messenger's guidance in courtesy, they would have come out of this crisis and received a life of plenty. If you adorned yourself with this etiquette in the matter of food and drink, a morsel or two would suffice you, and the most delicious food is that eaten after hunger, however simple it may be.

But now we see people resorting to appetizers before meals and to digestives after them. Why? Because they have contravened the guidance of their Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace: they eat when full, and they eat after being full.

The Truth, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive...﴾ (31) [al-A'raf]. And it is related of the Arabs, who lived in hardship, that they said: "Hunger is the best condiment; yes, it is the true sauce (al-ghamus) and the first appetizer."

Returning to the status of prayer among the acts of worship, and why it is the pillar of the religion: the meaning of "Prayer is the pillar of the religion" and "Islam is built upon five"⁵ is that religion consists of other things, and these are its foundations and principles. When we trace these principles, we find that the first pillar, which is the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, can be said even once. As for zakat, it is not obligatory on the poor, so the poor does not pay it; likewise the sick does not fast, nor the traveller, nor the menstruating woman, and so on; likewise the pilgrimage is not obligatory except upon the one able to do it.

So: what is the constant pillar that accompanies every Muslim and never falls from him in any circumstance? It is prayer. Therefore it has taken up a large portion of time over the course of the day and night, and through it is the constant declaration of loyalty to God, exalted is He. Through it you distinguish the believer from one who is not a believer. If you see a person, for example, who does not fast, or does not pay zakat, or does not perform the pilgrimage, you may say that perhaps he is one of those with excuses, one unable to do so; but when you see a person who does not pray, and this has been repeated from him, you will inevitably doubt his Islam.

For this reason, prayer has merited this status among all acts of worship since the beginnings of the legislation. Do you not see that all the obligations of the religion were legislated through revelation, except prayer, which was legislated through direct address from God, exalted is He, to His Prophet, our master Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, during the Night Journey and Ascension?

We have previously given an example of this, and to God belongs the highest likeness, with the head of a workplace who issues his orders by different means according to the importance of what is commanded. He may suffice with initialling a paper, or he may dictate it, or the competent employee may ask him and he tells him by telephone; but if the matter is important, he summons him personally to his office and assigns him what he wants.

This summoning was an honour for our master the Messenger of God, through the nearness of the one addressed to the sender. So the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wished that the community of Muhammad not be deprived of a favour He bestowed upon Muhammad. It is as if He said: whoever of My servants wishes to draw near to Me as Muhammad drew near, [and he was] at two bow-lengths or nearer, let him pray.

The meaning of ﴿And establish the prayer...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut]: establishing a thing means performing it in the most complete manner that fulfils its purpose. So the prayer required is the prayer that meets its conditions, and which you establish as its Legislator intends it. ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut].

When the prayer meets its conditions, it forbids its performer from immorality and wrongdoing. So if you see a prayer that does not forbid its performer from immorality and wrongdoing, know that it is deficient in what God intended by its establishment, and in proportion to the deficiency will be the fruit of the prayer in its performer's conduct. It is as if your falling into some immorality and some wrongdoing is a precise indicator of the extent of your mastery of your prayer and your eagerness to complete and establish it.

The meaning of ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing...﴾ (45) [al-'Ankabut] is clear in the Prophet's saying, may God bless him and grant him peace, when it was said to him: "O Messenger of God, so-and-so prays, but his prayer does not stop him from immorality and wrongdoing." He said: "Leave him, for his prayer will stop him."⁶

The meaning here is that the matter is not a fixed cosmic law that never fails; rather it is a legislative command open to being obeyed,

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best, except for those of them who do wrong, and say: "We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you; our God and your God is one, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

Exalted is He, teaches us how to argue with the People of the Book. Before we speak about the varieties of argument in the Noble Qur'an, let us say: what is the meaning of jidal (argument)?

Jidal (argument): it is derived from jadl, which is twisting a thing so that it becomes firm after having been soft, just as we twist our ropes in the countryside. Cotton or wool, for example, is fluffy and takes up a wide space; when we want to take a thread from it, we gather some of its fibres so that they strengthen one another by being twisted around each other. By twisting threads we make ropes so that they are stronger, and the strength of a rope is in proportion to the purpose for which it is intended.

From jadl come jidal, jadal and mujadalah, and their meanings include hiwar (dialogue), hijaj (argumentation) and munazarah (debate). Its meaning is that there are two parties, each of which has a doctrine that it supports and defends in order to fitnah (win over, or sway) the other, that is, to turn it away from its doctrine to its own doctrine.

If the aim in the argument, or the hijaj, or the munazarah, is the truth, then this name suffices. But if the argument slips into mira' (contentious wrangling) or lajājah (obstinacy), then the aim is not the truth; rather, it is that one of the two parties overcome the other. Argument in this case has many names, among them the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿They persisted in their rebellion...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75].

But if we twist a fluffy thing until it becomes compact and gains strength from its compactness, do you make your opponent strong in argument? You are trying to strengthen yourself in confronting him. They said: when I forbid him from falsehood and turn him towards the side of truth, he strengthens his certainty in something that benefits him; it is as if he had been fluffed up, taking up a space larger than his size through the falsehood he was upon, and I have strengthened him with the truth.

In colloquial Arabic we say (so-and-so is puffed up over nothing), or we say (so-and-so is fluffing his feathers), as if he had taken up a space larger than his size.

Therefore we observe that prevailing in argument is not for the sake of mere argument; rather, your prevailing is for a truth that benefits others, strengthens them, and returns them to their natural size.

Or: jidal is derived from jidal, which is the ground, as when the strong throws the weak to the ground in a struggle, for example.

Argument takes place between two persons, each of whom has his opinion, which he is accustomed to, loves, and is convinced of. When you argue with him, you want to move him from the opinion he is accustomed to to your opinion, which he is not accustomed to and has not adopted. You are thus combining two things against him: you want to move him from what he has become accustomed to and adopted to what he is not accustomed to. So let it not be with a method he dislikes, lest you combine two harshnesses against him.

So you must, then, use gentleness and winning over with kindness, because advice is heavy, as Shawqi, may God have mercy on him, said: "Do not make it a mountain, nor send it as an argument." The advisor often appears to be superior to the one advised, and they say: truths are bitter, so borrow for them the lightness of expression; for you are moving your opponent away from what he is used to, so do not move him away from what he is used to by what he dislikes, but by what he loves.

A person may express one and the same reality in a way that is disliked, and express it in a way that is loved and that he finds comfortable, like the king who saw in his dream that all his teeth had fallen out, so he asked for someone to interpret for him what he had seen. The interpreter came and listened to him, then said: "The meaning of this dream, O my lord, is that all your family will die." The king was displeased with this interpretation and did not like it. They sent for another, who said: "This means you will be the longest-lived of your family." The king was pleased with his words. Here the meaning is one, but the manner of presentation is different.

A man entered upon another and found him weeping, and said: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I was seized unjustly." He wondered and said: "Then how about you, if you had been seized justly? Would you be laughing?" The meaning is that one who is seized unjustly should not grieve, because he has done nothing that disgraces him; it is more fitting to weep for one who is seized justly and rightly.

A man whose dear one had been killed sat shrieking and wailing. His companion came in to console him, and the man said: "My son has been killed unjustly." His companion said: "Praise be to God who made you the one who was killed and did not make you the killer."

So: soundness of reasoning and lightness of expression are important matters, and the one who argues must observe his manner of speech and seek the appropriate opportunity. Do not argue with your opponent while he is angry with you or while you are angry with him. They said: a man passed by and found a boy drowning in the sea, so he did not wait until he had taken off his clothes; he threw himself in and rescued the boy, then began to beat and slap him, and the boy was saying: "Thank you, may God bless you! Why?" Because he was harsh with him after rescuing him. But what would the state be had he stood on the shore, hurled insults at him and rebuked him? Why would he go into the sea when he does not know how to swim? Therefore the wise say: "Help first, then advise."

Thus our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, teaches us the principles and manners of argument, because He wants by this argument to bring people out of disbelief into faith, and from denial into certainty, and this is not achieved except through gentleness and softness, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best...﴾ [al-Nahl: 125].

He, Exalted is He, teaches us that argument has ranks according to the condition of the opponent. The one who denies the existence of God has a particular kind of argument; the one who believes in God's existence but says that He has a partner has another kind; the one who believes in God and says "I will follow my prophet and will not follow you" has another kind, specifically; and those who differ with you from among the people of your own religion have an argument that suits their condition.

So: argument has ranks that we observe in the style of the Qur'an. With what did He argue those who do not believe in the existence of a god? He said: ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Rather, they are not certain.﴾ [al-Tur: 35–36].

He brought to them the matter of creation, which is manifest and which no one has claimed, and no one dares to deny it, not even the polytheists and atheists; for they know the maker of even the most trivial of their crafts, and they acknowledge him for his craftsmanship. Even if it were a glass cup or even a pencil, every craft must have a craftsman suited to it.

Is not He who created the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon, and so on, more deserving that they acknowledge Him, Exalted is He, as Creator? They themselves are created, and they did not say "we created ourselves," nor did they say "others created us." Who, then, created them?

We have said: a claim is established for its maker as long as no contrary evidence stands against it. God, Exalted and Glorified is He, has declared openly, through His messengers, and in a Qur'an that is recited until the Day of Resurrection, and has made everyone hear: "I am the Creator of this universe." If a stubborn one says, "Then who created God?" we say: the One who created Him must announce Himself.

God, Exalted is He, has testified for Himself that there is no god but He: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but Him...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. And no one has said "I am the god." So those who deny the Creator have no right. This is in the argument with the atheists who deny the existence of God.

As for those who believe in the existence of God but take partners with Him, we argue with them in the following manner: are your partners with God unseen or witnessed? If they say: unseen, then God, Exalted is He, has testified for Himself to His oneness, and said: "I am One, having no partner." Where, then, were your partners?

Why did they not defend their divinity alongside God? Either they were not aware of this declaration, or they were aware and were unable to confront it. In both cases the attribute of divinity is negated from them. What kind of god is this, that is unaware of what goes on around him, or is too cowardly to confront his opponent?

If they say: our partners are idols, trees, stars and others, then these are made by their own hands, so how can they worship them? Moreover, these are gods without a method and without obligations; otherwise, with what did they command them, and from what did they forbid them? So their worship of them is void.

Then we ask those who take partners with God: do these whom you associate with God act upon things with a single power, or do they take turns over things, each able to do a specific thing?

If they act upon things with a single power, then one of them suffices, and the others are of no use. If they take turns over things, then each is able to do one thing and unable to do another, and a god is not incapable.

The Exalted has answered these with His words: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.﴾ [al-Isra': 42], meaning: they would have gone to Him, either to rebuke Him and call Him to account for how He took the matter for Himself, or to win His favour and assist Him.

And in another place: ﴿Since each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91].

Having explained the argument with the atheists who deny the existence of a god and the argument with the polytheists, we argue with the People of the Book, who are gentler than their predecessors, because they believe in a god and that He is the Creator, and they believe in the message from God, and they believe in the books that were sent down. The difference between us and them is that they do not believe in the prophethood of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, whereas we believe in their messengers and their books. This is the first distinction by which Islam is distinguished from the other religions.

We say to them: you have believed in your messenger, and messengers came before him, so why do you deny that a messenger should come after him? Moreover, did the messenger come after your messenger to contradict him in the fundamentals of things? They all agree on the fundamentals of belief and morality; they all agree that they are servants of God who love one another; so why do you differ?

So our Lord, Blessed and Exalted is He, teaches us: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best...﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46], because they are neither atheists nor polytheists; they believe in your God, in the messengers, and in the books; the furthest that remains is that they do not believe in your messenger.

For this reason some people object: how does Islam permit a Muslim man to marry a woman from the People of the Book, but does not permit a Muslim woman to marry a man from the People of the Book? We say: because the basis of qawamah (guardianship) in marriage belongs to the man, and a believing husband who marries a woman of the People of the Book believes in her messenger; whereas a husband from the People of the Book does not believe in the messenger of the believing woman. The difference between them is great.

The meaning of ﴿except in a way that is best...﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46] is that in argument there is good and better. Good argument has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ [Saba': 24]. Nuh, peace be upon him, was gentle in arguing with his people, saying: ﴿If I have invented it, upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit.﴾ [Hud: 35].

He attributes the fabrication to himself and charges himself with the crime if he fabricated it—though he did not fabricate it, and it is they who are the criminals.

And our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, says in arguing with his people: ﴿Say: You will not be asked about what we committed, nor will we be asked about what you do.﴾ [Saba': 25]. He, may God bless him and grant him peace, mentions the crime with respect to himself and does not mention it with respect to the obstinate deniers. What manner of courtesy in calling to God is higher than this courtesy?

So: argue with those who do not believe in a good manner, and argue with the People of the Book in the way that is best, because of what distinguishes them from others, namely the belief in God. If they transgress and wrong themselves in the matter of the highest point of faith, by claiming that God has a son or something else, then by this they enter the ranks of their predecessors among the polytheists. If we are commanded to argue with them in the way that is best, and they say this statement, then we must argue with them by what is the opposite of the best: we argue with them either with the good, or with other than the good, that is, with the sword.

But can the sword impose beliefs? The sword takes from people only their outward forms.

As for hearts, nothing subdues them except faith, and God, Exalted is He, does not want forms; He wants hearts.

Read His words in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not believe. If We willed, We could send down upon them a sign from the heaven, so their necks would remain humbled before it.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3–4]. If He, Exalted is He, had willed to overpower forms and hearts into submission, so that no one could refuse faith as long as there was a disbeliever, then the disbeliever would not have disbelieved; rather, God gave him the faculty of choice. So the Exalted wants from us hearts that love Him and worship Him, because He, Exalted is He, deserves to be worshipped.

So: those who go outside the scope of being People of the Book by their excess, and by their saying that Jesus is the son of God, or that God is the third of three, they only enter the scope of polytheism and disbelief. We will not say to these: follow our messenger; rather, follow your messenger and the book that came to you from God. You will find in it the good news of Muhammad, {the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered, whom they find written with them in the Torah}.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5340):
((The scholars differed concerning the words of the Exalted: {And do not argue with the People of the Book... [al-'Ankabut: 46]}.
Mujahid said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), so it is permissible to argue with the People of the Book in the way that is best, in the sense of calling them to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and drawing attention to His proofs and signs, hoping for their acceptance of faith, not by way of harshness and coarseness.
It was said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of fighting: His words {Fight those who do not believe in God... [al-Tawbah: 29]}.))
Then al-Qurtubi said: ((Mujahid's view is good, because the rulings of God, Mighty and Majestic, are not said to be abrogated except by something clear that removes the excuse, or by an argument from reason. Ibn al-'Arabi chose this view.))

Then the Truthful (Exalted is He) says:

﴿And thus We have sent down to you the Book. Those to whom We gave the Book believe in it, and among these there are some who believe in it. And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers.﴾ (29:47)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have sent down to you the Book..﴾ (29:47). That is: just as We sent down books to those before you, We have sent down to you a Book that carries a method (manhaj). The heavenly books are of two kinds. One kind carries the Messenger's method in (do this) and (do not do this), and this is common to all the books sent down to the messengers. The second is a single book, the Qur'an, which came with the method and the miracle together.

Every messenger before Muhammad (ﷺ) had a book containing a method, and a miracle separate from that method. Moses (peace be upon him) had the Torah as his book, and his miracle was the staff. Jesus (peace be upon him) had the Gospel as his book, and his miracle was raising the dead by God's permission.

As for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his book is the Qur'an and his miracle is the Qur'an. So observe how the miracle was joined with the method so that it would remain attached to it, because the time of Muhammad's mission extends until the Hour arrives. The miracle must therefore remain present, so that people can say: Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and this is his miracle.

By contrast, we cannot, for example, say: This is Jesus, the Messenger of God, and this is his miracle, because it no longer remains, and we know it only through the Qur'an's report of it. This clarifies for us the excellence of the Qur'an over the messengers and their miracles, since it establishes them for everyone who did not see them: everyone who believes in the Qur'an believes in them.

But does every messenger come with his miracle? The miracle comes only for one who has challenged a people and accused him of lying, so that the miracle comes to confirm his truthfulness in conveying from his Lord. Therefore we find, for example, that Shaytha (Seth), Idris and Shu'ayb (peace be upon them) had no miracles.

And did Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) and Lady Khadija, Mother of the Believers, need a miracle to believe in the Messenger of God? Never. As soon as he said, "I am the Messenger of God," they believed in him. So what need was there for a miracle then?

Thus, the Prophet (ﷺ) was distinguished from his fellow messengers in that his book is itself his miracle. We have said before that God, blessed and exalted, makes the miracle of the same kind as that in which the people excel. Had He challenged them with something they had no knowledge of, they would have said: "We do not know this, so how can You challenge us with it?" The Arabs were a people of eloquence and expression, and they set up markets and gatherings for speech. So He challenged them with the eloquence and rhetoric of the Qur'an to produce its like, then to produce ten surahs, then one surah, and they were unable to do so. The Qur'an is speech of the same kind as their speech, with the same letters and words, except that the one who speaks the Qur'an is God, Exalted is He; therefore no one can produce its like.

The Qur'an is also a book that holds sway (muhaymin) over all the books before it: it retains from them whatever rulings He wills and abrogates whatever He wills. As for beliefs, they are fixed and there is no abrogation (naskh) in them, and likewise there is no abrogation in narratives and reports.

Abrogation comes only in legislation, in the rulings of do and do not do, because legislation comes suited to the ailments of different environments.

Hence some messengers were contemporaries, such as Abraham and Lot, and Moses and Shu'ayb (peace be upon them), each with his own mission, because each was directed to a particular place to treat a particular ailment, in a time when the means of contact between different environments were cut off, so a community in one place might not know of others in a neighbouring environment.

As for Muhammad (ﷺ), he came, as his Lord knew from eternity, at an appointed time when environments would meet and civilisations would intermingle. The event takes place at the end of the world, so we learn of it, indeed we witness it in the moment as it happens, as though it were in our own land. Therefore the ailments will also be united, and since the ailments of the various nations have become one, one messenger suffices to treat them, and he is a messenger to all mankind.

Then He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book..﴾ (29:47), that is, those before you: ﴿believe in it..﴾ (29:47), because no temporal authority isolates them from the new Book, so they examine the descriptions of the new Prophet that appear in their books and match them against the descriptions of the Messenger of God. Thus when Salman al-Farisi (1) heard that there was a new prophet in Mecca, he went to the Messenger of God and began to contemplate him and look at him closely. He found in him two of the signs mentioned in the earlier books: that he (ﷺ) accepts gifts and does not accept charity. So he began looking here and there, perhaps he would see the third. The Messenger of God perceived him through the prophetic insight God had placed in him, and said: "Perhaps you want this," and he uncovered for him the Seal of Prophethood, which is the third sign (2).

And among the graciousness of our master Abdullah ibn Salam, when he went to the Messenger of God while still a Jew, he said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews are a people of slander (bahat), meaning they multiply disputation to no avail, and I fear that if I announce my Islam they will revile me, wrong me, and say vile things about me. So I wish, O Messenger of God, that when they come to you, you would ask them about me; then, when they say what they say, I will announce my Islam." When a group of Jews came to the Messenger of God, he asked them: "What do you say of Abdullah ibn Salam?" They said: "Our shaykh, our rabbi, our master..." etc. Abdullah said: "Since they have said what they said, O Messenger of God, I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that you are the Messenger of God." Immediately they said: "Rather, you are our evil and the son of our evil," and they reviled him. Abdullah said: "Did I not tell you, O Messenger of God, that they are a people of slander (3)?"

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among these there are some who believe in it..﴾ (29:47), that is, among the disbelievers of Mecca there are those who will come after these and believe in the Qur'an. ﴿And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers..﴾ (29:47). Jahd (denial) is deliberate rejection, for rejection may arise from ignorance, for example, whereas jahd arises when the tongue affirms while the heart negates, or the tongue negates while the heart affirms; this is what we call juhud.

Therefore the Qur'an distinguishes between the wording of the utterance and the inner feelings of the soul. Read, for example, the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of God..﴾ (63:1). This is a fine and beautiful statement from them, ﴿and God knows that you are indeed His Messenger..﴾ (63:1), that is, their words agreed with God's knowledge. But ﴿God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ (63:1). How then does the Truth judge them to be liars, when they said what agreed with God's knowledge?

We say: God's speech requires reflection on its meaning. The Truth judges them liars not in their saying "You are indeed the Messenger of God," which is true, but in their testimony, because it is a testimony by the tongue that is not matched by belief in the heart. What is attested is true, but the testimony is false.

Why, then, did He single out the disbelievers in the matter of jahd? They said: because a non-disbeliever has an awakened conscience, so he does not dare utter this word, for he knows that God does not seize people for their sins now, but postpones them to the Day of Reckoning, and this consideration restrains them from jahd.

(1) Salman al-Farisi, a Companion, one of their foremost. His origin was from the Magians of Isfahan. He lived a long life, read the books of Persia, Rome and the Jews, travelled to the lands of the Arabs, heard the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), and declared his Islam. He is the one who guided the Muslims to dig the trench in the Battle of the Confederates. He died in 36 AH in al-Mada'in, where he was governor. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 3/112].

(2) al-Bayhaqi related the story of Salman al-Farisi's Islam in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa over 18 pages (1/82–100). In it, when he met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and saw that he ate gifts and did not accept charity, Salman went around behind the Messenger of God, saying: "The Prophet (ﷺ) noticed me, so he loosened his garment, and there was the Seal in the upper part of his left shoulder. I recognised it, then I moved around and sat before him, and I said: I bear witness that there is no god but God and that you are the Messenger of God."

(3) Related by al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa (2/526–529), and by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3911), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him).

The commentary on surah 29, verse 48:

His words, ﴿You did not recite before it any book⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut]: "recite" means read. He chose *tatlu* (تتلو, recite) because you do not read except what you have heard. Your reading of what you heard makes your speech "*tali*" (تاليا, following) what you heard. We say *yatluhu*, meaning: it comes after it. ﴿Nor did you write it with your right hand⁠﴾: meaning, writing.

There is a difference between reading and writing. A person may read because he has memorised, and memorisation results from hearing. Like our brothers whom God tested with loss of sight, who still read, reading only what they have heard. As we have said, hearing is the first sense to perform its function in a human being, so it is possible to memorise what you have heard. But to write it down is something else.

The discourse here is a kind of argument and persuasion directed at the disbelievers of Quraysh who denied the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and also a kind of consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is as if God, glorified be He, says to His Messenger: Be reassured. Their denial of you is a fabrication against you, because you had not recited any book before it, nor written one with your right hand, and they know your conduct among them.

As He, glorified be He, said in another place: ﴿I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it, will you not reason?⁠﴾ [Yunus]

Forty years the Messenger of God spent among his people before the commissioning (*bi'tha*, the start of his prophethood). They never found him reading, writing, delivering speeches, or composing a poem. So how do you deny him now?

If they say: it was genius in Muhammad, which remained hidden until he reached forty. We say: genius usually appears in the late second decade of life, at seventeen or eighteen. And who guaranteed Muhammad survival until forty, while he saw the deaths of his family, his grandfather, his father and his mother?

Had you possessed any reading or writing, they would have had an excuse, and there would have been a doubt that called for suspicion about your affair, as they said: ﴿Fables of the ancients, which he has had written down, and which are dictated to him morning and evening⁠﴾ [Al-Furqan].

They also said: ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him⁠﴾ [Al-Nahl 103]. The Qur'an replied to them: ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic⁠﴾ [Al-Nahl 103] (1).

They said: he is a sorcerer. They said: he is a poet. They said: he is possessed. All of these are fabrications and worthless falsehoods that are easy to refute. If he were a sorcerer, why did he not bewitch you too, and the matter end? If he were a poet, did you ever find him composing poetry before his commissioning?

If you say he is possessed: possession is the loss of reason, such that a person cannot choose between alternatives. Have you ever found Muhammad to have anything of that? How can a possessed man be of tremendous character, when you yourselves testify that he is the truthful, the trustworthy? He has discipline in his faculties and in his conduct. So how can you accuse him of possession?

The word ﴿before it⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48] has marvels in the Book of God. Among them is this verse: ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor write it with your right hand⁠﴾. Some of the knowledgeable say: "before it" means before the Qur'an was revealed to you. This phrase ﴿before it⁠﴾ indicates that it is permissible that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had learned how to read and how to write after the Qur'an was revealed to him, so that no one in his community would be better than him in anything, or in virtues of goodness (2).

Then consider His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of God before?⁠﴾ [Al-Baqarah 91]. By God, if this verse had come without the word "before" (*min qabl*), would it not enter the mind of the Messenger of God that they might be emboldened against him and kill him, so that he would be apprehensive of them? Or would it enter their own minds, so that they would be emboldened against him as they had killed the prophets before? Therefore the verse came to establish that this happened in the past, while now nothing of this will ever happen, and God will never enable you against His Prophet.

The phrase ﴿I was not⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48] recurs often in the Book of God, and they call it "the *ma kunta* phrases of the Qur'an". In it is evidence that the Qur'an broke through all the veils of past, present and future time.

As in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses⁠﴾ [Al-Qasas 44].

And His saying: ﴿You did not dwell among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses⁠﴾ [Al-Qasas 45].

And His saying: ﴿You were not with them when they cast their pens, to see which of them would take charge of Maryam⁠﴾ [Al Imran 44].

And here: ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor write it with your right hand⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48].

For this reason his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, described him as ﴿the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered⁠﴾ [Al-A'raf 157]. Beware of supposing that being unlettered (*ummiyya*, unlettered) is a defect in the Messenger of God. If it is a defect in others, it is a nobility in him. The meaning of *ummi* is that he remains in his natural state as his mother bore him. He learned nothing from anyone. Likewise the Messenger of God did not learn from creation; he learned from the Creator, and so the rank of his knowledge was raised above creation.

Among this is the standing that Imam 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, held in knowledge and in issuing legal rulings (*ifta'*). 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said of him, despite what was known of 'Umar's soundness of judgement, to the point that the Qur'an would be revealed in agreement with his opinion and in support of his statement: "Wretched is the place in a land where there is no Abu al-Hasan" (3). Why?

Because he was a man of argument and logic, and a man of eloquence. Did he not argue with al-Faruq over the matter of the woman who gave birth after six months from her husband, when 'Umar wished to impose the prescribed punishment on her? It was commonly held that the period of pregnancy is nine months, so some were hasty and said she had committed fornication. But 'Ali had a different opinion, and said to 'Umar: "But God says otherwise." 'Umar said: "And what is that?" He said: "Did not the Truthful, exalted be He, say: ﴿The mothers breastfeed their children for two complete years⁠﴾ [Al-Baqarah 233]?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "Did He not say: ﴿Its carrying and its weaning are thirty months⁠﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 15]? Subtract the two years from thirty months and what remains is six months. So if a woman gives birth at six months, this is a natural matter with no doubt about it" (4).

One day Hudhayfah entered upon 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both. 'Umar asked him: "How have you risen this morning, Hudhayfah?" Hudhayfah said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I have risen loving trial, disliking truth, praying without ablution, and I have in the earth what God does not have in the heavens."

'Umar became angry and intended to strike him with a whip (*durra*) in his hand. Then 'Ali entered and found 'Umar angry. He said: "What is it that I see you angry, O Commander of the Faithful?" 'Umar recounted to him what had happened with Hudhayfah. 'Ali said:

"Yes, O Commander of the Faithful, he loves trial, because God, exalted be He, said: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial⁠﴾ [Al-Taghabun 15]. He dislikes truth, meaning death, for it is a truth, but we dislike it. He prays without ablution, meaning he prays upon the Prophet (ﷺ) without ablution. He has in the earth a child and a wife, and God does not have that in the heavens." Then 'Umar said his famous saying: "Wretched is the place in a land where there is no Abu al-Hasan."

Why did 'Ali distinguish himself with this quality of knowledge, jurisprudence and argument? Because he was raised in the lap of prophethood, and drew from its source, and grew up in the embrace of Islamic sciences from his earliest youth. He did not know anything of the information of the Jahiliyya (the time of ignorance). So when Islamic sciences interact within him, they give birth only to truth.

Then He, exalted be He, says: ﴿Otherwise⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48], meaning: if you had reading or writing, ﴿the falsifiers would have doubted⁠﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48]. That is, they would have had an excuse and a viewpoint for doubting. Doubt here does not mean mere suspicion; it is doubt accompanied by accusation. That is, they accuse the Messenger of God of having knowledge of reading and writing. Therefore He described them as falsifiers in their accusing him (ﷺ).

(1) Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to teach a smith in Mecca named Balam, who spoke a non-Arabic tongue. The polytheists would see the Messenger of God (ﷺ) enter upon him and leave from his presence, so they said: "It is only Balam who teaches him." So God revealed: ﴿We know that they say: it is only a human being who teaches him⁠﴾ [Al-Nahl 103]. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/167) and attributed it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh with a weak chain.

(2) Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5241): "Al-Naqqash mentioned in his tafsir of this verse, from al-Sha'bi, that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not die until he wrote. He also supported with a chain the hadith of Abu Kabsha al-Sulami, whose content is that the Prophet (ﷺ) read a letter from 'Uyayna ibn Hisn and informed them of its meaning." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "All of this is weak." Then he said (7/5243): "The correct position on this matter is that he did not write, not even a single letter, but he commanded someone to write. Likewise he did not read, nor spell out words."

(3) Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (1/457), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: "We performed the pilgrimage with 'Umar, may God be pleased with him. When he entered the circumambulation he faced the Black Stone and said: 'I know that you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits.'" It is a long hadith, and in it 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "I seek refuge with God, exalted be He, from living among a people in whom you are not present, O Abu al-Hasan."

(4) Al-Jassas in Ahkam al-Qur'an (3/517) mentioned that this event occurred in the time of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. But it seems these are two incidents, which occurred in the times of each of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi, in his book al-Mughni (9/115), mentioned that it was in the time of 'Umar, and cited what al-Athram narrated with his chain from Abu al-Aswad, and recounted the story.

(5) From Ma'mar ibn 'Abdullah al-Juhani who said: A man among us married a woman from Juhayna, and she gave birth to a child exactly six months later. Her husband went to 'Uthman and mentioned this to him. He sent for her, and when she stood up to put on her clothes, her sister wept. She said: "What makes you weep? By God, no one has touched me ever except him. God decrees in what He wills." When 'Uthman brought her, he ordered her stoning. This reached 'Ali, so he came to him and said: "What are you doing?" He said: "She gave birth to a complete child at six months. Is that possible?" 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "Do you not read the Qur'an?" "Yes." He said: "Did you not hear God, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿Its carrying and its weaning are thirty months⁠﴾ [Al-Ahqaf 15], and He said: ﴿two complete years⁠﴾ [Al-Baqarah 233]? So we find that only six months remain." 'Uthman said: "By God, I did not notice this. Bring me the woman." They found that she had already been dealt with. Cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (4/157).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 29, verse 49:

﴿Bal﴾ (Nay, rather) is a particle that indicates a turning away from what precedes it and an emphasis on what follows it. ﴿He﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾. He said ﴿in the breasts﴾ and did not say, for example, "in their memory," because the ear receives speech and presents it to the intellect; but when it reaches the heart, it settles in the heart and in the breast, and there it turns into conviction and into certainty that admits no doubt and cannot be moved.

Therefore, the Exalted says about the Qur'an: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:193–194]. So He said ﴿upon your heart﴾, i.e., directly it settled in his heart, and He did not say "upon your ear."

Then Allah, exalted is He, says:

{ They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner." 50 }

That is, after the Qur'an had come to them and had left them powerless, they ask for other signs. We have already said that when a people proposed a sign to their messenger and Allah answered their request, then if they denied after it, He would seize them with the seizure of the Mighty, the Powerful.

Consider His saying, for example: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a clear sign, but they wronged themselves through it﴾ (Al-Isra 17:59). When they denied the sign they had asked for, Allah destroyed them. The matter, then, is not one of signs and persuasion. It is insistence on disbelief. So the sending down of a particular sign at their suggestion does not prevent them from disbelieving in the Messenger of Allah as well.

Therefore He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We did not refrain from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ (Al-Isra 17:59). That is, the signs they had proposed. When a sign is sent down and they deny it, the punishment of heaven descends upon them. But the Truth (al-Haqq), exalted is He, made a covenant to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) that He would not punish his community while he was among them, as He said: ﴿Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:33).

This, then, is the reason that prevents the proposed sign from coming. Moreover, the proposed signs are cosmic signs that come and go, like a matchstick you light once, after which it goes out. Whoever saw it saw it, and it became a report for those who did not see it.

The word ﴿لولا﴾ (lawla) is used in Arabic in two ways. If it enters a nominal sentence, as in "lawla Zayd 'indaka lazurtuka" (Had it not been for Zayd with you, I would have visited you), it is a particle of prohibition due to existence: the visit was prevented because Zayd was present. If it enters a verbal sentence, as in "lawla tudhakkiru duroosak" (Why do you not review your lessons?), it expresses urging and exhortation to act.

So their saying ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:50) is as if the sign that had come to them from Allah were not something they acknowledged. Then they contradict themselves when they say: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ (Al-Zukhruf 43:31).

So you acknowledge the Qur'an and are convinced by it, but what sticks in your throats is that it should be sent down upon Muhammad from among all people. Then we see them contradicting themselves in this too, and admitting without realising it that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, when they said: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse﴾ (Al-Munafiqun 63:7). As long as you know that he is the Messenger of Allah, why do you oppose him? The innate, self-evident nature denies them, and the Truth speaks through their tongues when they are heedless.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, answers them: ﴿Say, "The signs are only with Allah"﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:50). They are with Allah, not with me, and they are not something to be demanded according to your whims. ﴿I am only a clear warner﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:50). That is, this is my task. He chose the word "warner" although he (ﷺ) is both a bearer of glad tidings and a warner. But here He singled them out with warning, because they are a people of contention, of falsehood and of denial, so the word "warner" suits them rather than "bearer of glad tidings."

¹ Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5245): "Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿āyah﴾ (sign) in the singular. The others read it in the plural. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because of Allah's saying: ﴿Say, "The signs are only with Allah"﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:50)..."

Then the Exalted says:

{Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.} (29:51)

The interrogative here is for amazement and denial. That is: how is the Qur'an not sufficient for them, nor convincing to them, when it is the greatest of signs? It has rendered them unable to produce even one sign like its signs, and it has brought them much admonition and wonder. Thus, they wish to be obstinate and not to believe. Had they been seekers of truth, searching for guidance, one verse of the Qur'an would have been sufficient for them to believe in it.

As for His saying, ﴿recited to them﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would receive revelation of several verses, which might extend to a quarter or three-quarters [of a juz']. When the inspiration left him, he would recite what had been revealed to him to his Companions so that they might write it down. He would recite it just as it was revealed to him, and the scribes would write it, and whoever among them memorised it would memorise it. They were a people of transmission and a people of memorisation.

Then the time of prayer would come, and the Messenger of Allah would lead them in prayer with the verses that had been revealed to him, repeating them as he had received them. This was a divine gift granted to His Messenger (ﷺ), and He addressed him with the words: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ (87:6).

Otherwise, you may challenge the people with the best memory to repeat to you a sermon or a speech you delivered over, say, half an hour, and then repeat it to you exactly as you said it the first time.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder﴾ (29:51), but [it is] for ﴿a people who believe﴾ (29:51), because the Qur'an bears fruit only in those who receive it well and believe in it. As for those who do not believe, it is in their ears a deafness, and it is for them a blindness; they neither comprehend it nor reflect upon it, because they receive it not with a pure soul but with hatred and aversion, so they gain neither its light, nor its blessing, nor its guidance.

Therefore, Allah the Exalted says of those who receive the speech of Allah well: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing﴾ (41:44).

As for those who deny it and do not receive it well, He says of them: ﴿And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is for them a blindness﴾ (41:44).

We have previously said that the act is one, but the recipients differ. We illustrated this with one who blows on his hands to warm them in the cold, and one who blows on tea to cool it, and you too blow on a candle to extinguish it, and blow on a fire to kindle it.

In another place the Exalted says: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾ (17:82). He distinguishes between healing (shifa') and mercy (rahmah). Healing means that there was an ailment and it has been cured; but mercy means that the ailment does not return to you, and the disease does not come upon you again. The Qur'an was revealed to treat spiritual diseases: it treats them through recitation and fortifies you against them so that they do not afflict you. If you fall into any of these diseases, recite what the Qur'an has said about them, for they will be cured by the permission of Allah. Thus, healing treats the disease if it occurs through heedlessness of the soul's conduct.

If we applied the matters of the Qur'an to our souls, this mercy would reach us. Man is body, values, meanings and morals; these meanings in man are called the psyche (nafsiyyat). A person may be sound in physical constitution and body, yet sick in soul. Therefore, among the medical specialties we find psychiatry, and every patient for whose illness they find no organic cause, they diagnose as a psychological illness. When you ask the psychiatrist, you find that all he has are drugs that calm the patient or subdue him so that he sleeps and does not think of anything. Is this the treatment?

If we reflect on the Book of our Lord, we find in it both treatments: the physical and the psychological. The soundness of the body lies in that Allah the Exalted has made lawful for you some things and forbidden you others, and you need only walk straight upon the path of your Lord to be spared the diseases of the body. If you are one of those who love eating what is lawful but go to excess in it to the point of surfeit, then read in the Qur'an: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive; indeed He does not like the excessive﴾ (7:31).

Then you find in the Prophetic Sunnah an explanatory reminder of this verse: "The son of Adam does not fill a vessel worse than his stomach. It is sufficient for the son of Adam to have a few morsels to keep his back upright; if he must do more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath."(2)

The principle, then, is that man eats in order to live, not that he lives in order to eat. Some superficial people say: what is meant by "a third for his breath"? Is the breath in the stomach? Now, with the development of the sciences, we know that overeating of the belly presses upon the diaphragm and constricts the space of the lungs, resulting in shortness of breath.

As for the psychological aspect, psychological illness arises either from the contraction of the faculties from their natural constitution, or their expansion beyond their natural constitution. Like the egg, for example, which has a specific size: if you constrict this size or stretch it, it breaks.

This is also the root of disease in the human soul, because the faculties of the soul ought to remain in a state of balance and equilibrium. You find this balance in the method of your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, where He says: ﴿So that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you﴾ (57:23).

So ﴿so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you﴾ (57:23) means contraction, and ﴿nor exult over what He has given you﴾ (57:23) means expansion. Both are blameworthy and forbidden. But who is there who does not grieve over what has passed, nor rejoice over what is yet to come?

Therefore, we find that the dullards, whom events do not shake, have strong health, because they do not grieve excessively. Indeed, the poets did not overlook this meaning, as one of them says:

"In dullness is the same strength as in resolve.
Indeed the dull one is strong of soul, stubborn."
Ask the people of resolve, if their resolves falter,
Whether the mountains' foundations have trembled over dullness?

So what you take for dullness is a strong resolve in receiving events and standing firm against them.

Thus: mercy in Allah's method, if we adhere to it, keeps us safe from ailments, whether they are physical or moral.

(1) Cause of revelation of the verse: "It has been said that the cause of revelation of these verses is what Ibn 'Uyayna narrated... He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a shoulder-blade on which there was writing, and he said: 'Sufficient for a people in error is that they turn away from what their Prophet brought to what another prophet brought, or another book than their book.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book...﴾ (29:51)." Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5245).
(2) On the authority of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No son of Adam fills a vessel worse than his stomach. It is sufficient for the son of Adam to have a few morsels to keep his back upright; if he must do more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2380), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (3349).
(3) Asaytu 'alayhi asan: al-asa is grief. Asaytu li-fulan: I grieved for so-and-so. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: asa]
(4) From the poetry of Shaykh Ridwan, may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 29, verse 52:

{ Say, "Allah suffices as a witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — it is they who are the losers." }

(Say) i.e., to those who deny you: ﴿Allah suffices as a witness between me and you.﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:52] i.e., it is enough for me that Allah bears witness for me that I have conveyed (the message). Your testimony is of no benefit to me, just as your faith does not benefit me and your disbelief does not harm me. My reward is taken from my Lord for merely conveying, and I have conveyed, and Allah has borne witness to that for me.

In another place He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you."﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:43] i.e., you have not been content with the signs, nor have you believed in them, but I am content with the Lord of these signs as a witness between me and you. Thus, there is a dispute over the conveying (of the message) between Muhammad ﷺ and his people, who deny him in conveying from his Lord.

So there must necessarily be a settling of this dispute. When we look at human matters of litigation, we find that either the accused confesses, or a witness of truth testifies, not a witness of falsehood, and then the matter is presented to the judge to rule on the basis of the testimony or the evidence.

The judge must not be one who follows his desires. Then comes the stage of executing the ruling, which is the executive authority, and this too should have no desires, so that it executes the ruling as it truly is. Thus, human disputes pass through multiple stages, and the truths may become blurred if the necessary conditions are not met for these parties. If the witness testifies falsely, or the judge is biased, or the executor of the ruling carries it out deceptively, the matters would be overturned.

As for the judgment of the Truth — glory be to Him, the Exalted — in the dispute between Muhammad and his people, He, glory be to Him, is sufficient as Judge, Arbiter, and Executor. Why? Because He, glory be to Him: ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:52]

Nothing hidden on earth or in heaven is concealed from Him. He knows the secret and what is more hidden. So what testimony is more just than His? He, glory be to Him, is a just judge who rules by the truth, because He has no desire that inclines Him toward falsehood, and He, glory be to Him, does not alter the execution of judgments, because He executes His own judgment.

So who is the winner in a judgment whose judge is the Truth — blessed and exalted is He — and whose parties to the dispute are Muhammad and his people? The Messenger of Allah won in that Allah is the Witness, and the disbelievers lost when they disbelieved in Him, and the clear proof that came to them in the noble Qur'an did not suffice them.

The knowledge of Allah of the unseen is not a matter of treatment and study to learn; rather, affairs come at a timing from Him, pre-eternal from eternity, and the world manifests in accordance with what He has willed from eternity. Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:82]

That is, He says to the thing, as if it already exists, awaiting the command from Allah to appear to people. So His saying "Be" is only for manifestation. As for the matter of creation, it is concluded from eternity, and the "blueprint" (al-maketh, a modern term for the design/model) exists. Thus the Truth, glory be to Him, knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, but we do not even know the unseen of ourselves.

He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:7] Is there anything more hidden than the secret? They said: the secret is what you conceal within yourself, and what is more hidden than it is that He knows it before it exists within yourself.

Some have paused at His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He knows what you reveal and what you conceal.﴾ [al-Nur 24:29] and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He knows what is openly declared of speech and He knows what you conceal.﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:110]

They say: what is the aspect of Allah's favour in knowing what is openly declared of speech, and knowing what we reveal, since this is something not hidden that everyone knows?

We say: understand from Allah His intent. The meaning is not that He, glory be to Him, said: "I know what you alone reveal, nor what you alone declare aloud," but rather what all of you reveal, and what all of you declare aloud. To clarify this matter, imagine a demonstration of several hundred or several thousand people in which chants and voices intermingle and words overlap, such that you cannot distinguish the voice of one from the voice of another.

But the Truth, glory be to Him, can distinguish these voices and return each one to its owner. Therefore, in demonstrations, we see that each person can say whatever he wishes and chant what he would not dare chant alone, because his voice will mix with the voices and be concealed within them, so its source is not known. Thus the knowledge of the openly declared is stronger than the knowledge of the unseen.

If you say: some scholars, through their discoveries and research, have reached knowledge of secrets that were hidden in the universe, such as electricity, the atom, and others, so they thereby know the unseen. We say: yes, they knew something that was hidden in the universe, but they knew it through premises that Allah created and facilitated for them. They took these premises and reached their discoveries through them, just as your son, for example, solves a geometry problem by using the given data.

So, in reality, this is not unseen; rather it is something existing, but it has a birth and a time in which it appears. When its time comes, Allah facilitates for His creatures the means to reach it, either through research and using premises. When the birth of a secret coincides with the search of creation, it is said that they have encompassed some of Allah's unseen knowledge.

He, exalted be He, says: ﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.﴾ [al-Baqara 2:255] i.e., He willed that it be born.
